changes_made: Key finding 5: within-arm falls are reported for four of the five head-to-head trials, not Verachai 2014; time to cure (slightly favouring haloperidol) added; note on the Table 2/3 cross-reference.
Key finding 6: CGI-S 2 vs 2.1 has no stated time point; the placebo comparison is from Table 3 (p < 0.05), the text's p < 0.005 names no comparison.
Reporting issue 3: Verachai's SMD matches the GEE result, so it is a qualified example, not a contradiction.
Reporting issue 5: consequence corrected (the side-effect denominators fit neither the arms nor the completers).
Reporting issue 7: the 'dropout rate' cannot be cumulative dropout because it falls between day 27 and day 58.
Reporting issue 9: about 85% is possible for six trials (83%); the inconsistency is with the two high-risk trials.
Interpretation gap: results_show no longer says between-drug differences were mostly not significant; gap (3) says the Results do state haloperidol superiority (item-level, intervals including zero).
Exposure: the route is stated only for Sulaiman 2013.
New reporting issue 12: the per-source search counts sum to 838, not 643.
New reporting issue 13: Verachai cure rate (Table 3) and time to cure (text) point in opposite directions.
rejected: Reporting issue 6 (mean age 32, SD 20.63): the reader's bound for trials capped at 60 (SD at most about 19.8) is not added, because not every trial had an upper age limit (one enrolled from 15, one from 18 with no cap); the issue already says the SD is implausible.
for_senior_author: AMSTAR 2 single items, no effect on the overall (critically low from items 2 and 13): AI reader 21 calls item 7 (yes) generous, since a 2018 randomized trial cited in the discussion (Xue et al.) is neither included nor listed as excluded, and would accept yes on item 9 (Cochrane tool). Both readers agree on every item as recorded.

New reporting issue 13: the text calls lifetime methamphetamine use (89.70%) primary use.
New reporting issue 14: four percentage misprints in Tables 1 and 3.
for_senior_author: RoB 2 randomization domain (some concerns): AI reader 21 notes it would be high if allocation concealment is read as no information (opaque envelopes not described as sequentially numbered) given the large sex imbalance; the overall (high) is unchanged either way.

changes_made: Low symptom levels attributed: shown here only for Wang 2019; for Sulaiman 2013 from the network meta-analysis (key finding 5 note, cannot_establish, results_show).
Key finding 10: the paliperidone craving d (0.951) is within-arm; between-group p = 0.03 (paliperidone) and 0.015 (aripiprazole); editors' note on the misprinted SD.
Key finding 8 note: the 2026 and 2019 reviews disagree on Wang 2016's Simpson–Angus result.

Reporting issue 7: the same paragraph misquotes the Wang 2020 dose range (27% for 25%).
AMSTAR 2 item 4 partial yes → no (unjustified restriction to peer-reviewed literature, applied as written); overall low → critically low; reasoning recomputed.
for_senior_author: The overall changed from low to critically low only because AMSTAR 2 item 4 was applied as written to an unjustified restriction to peer-reviewed literature (the review has no language limit). Senior decision 21 concerns language limits; if the senior author reads publication restrictions as covering only language, item 4 returns to partial yes and the card to low confidence. Both readers agree on every other item.

Interpretation gap: AI reader 21 rates it substantial rather than minor (the abstract's conclusion that the review found support for the effectiveness of antipsychotics rests on within-arm changes labelled huge and on two small placebo-controlled trials in stabilised or improving people; the cautious Conclusion section does not reach the abstract; compare senior decision 23 on Boden 2023). Left at minor, the first reader's rating; a single-field judgment that does not affect the card status.

changes_made: AMSTAR 2 item 4 partial yes → no (peer-reviewed only and grey literature excluded without a reason, applied as written); overall low → critically low (provisional on item 7); reasoning recomputed.
Interpretation gap and key finding 5: no categorical moderator met the threshold; older cohorts had lower transition in meta-regression (P = .0286).

for_senior_author: The overall changed from low to critically low (provisional on item 7) because AMSTAR 2 item 4 was applied as written: the search was limited to peer-reviewed publications and grey literature was excluded without a reason (only the English-language limit is explained). This matches AI reader 21's overall; the first reader's note that a strict reading would not change the overall was an arithmetic slip under the card's own counting of item 7. On a lenient reading of publication restrictions the first reader's low (provisional) would return, and the readers would then disagree on the overall through item 11.

AMSTAR 2 item 11 (single item): AI reader 21 would rate it no (pooling cumulative proportions over 1 to 20 years with I² of 96% to 99% is not justified in the text; no prediction intervals); the first reader judged it met on balance, a close call. Kept as yes. It changes the overall only if the unopened supplement turns out to list the 141 excluded full texts with reasons.

Optional, editors' calculation now on the card: Table 3 implies that the Thai cohort entered the analyses with about 449 people (its followed-up 40%), so its 39% is probably a share of those followed up; the course claim could say so if the senior author wants it there (it would need anchor 19's extracted text extended).

amstar2_item4.rule_applied: AMSTAR 2 item 4 gives partial yes only if at least two databases were searched, keywords or a strategy are given, and publication restrictions such as language are justified. Applied as written, as batch 3 did (sc_voce_2019 counted its published-only limit too): any publication restriction without a stated reason, language or publication status, gives no; the overall was recomputed from the critical items.

this_batch.item4: partial-yes (no language, date or publication-status limit; unaffected)
partial-yes → no (eligibility restricted to peer-reviewed literature without a reason; no language limit)
partial-yes → no (peer-reviewed publications only and grey literature excluded without a reason; the English-language limit is explained)

earlier_cards_to_check.reason: Its item 4 note lists 'published data only' among the shortfalls for yes. If that is an eligibility restriction without a stated reason, item 4 applied as written is no; its source was not read in this round.
earlier_cards_to_check.overall_effect: low-confidence → critically-low (item 7 is already not met)

amstar2_item4.for_senior_author: Senior decision 21 is worded for language limits. Hall 2026 and Murrie 2020 are the first cards whose overall turns on an unjustified publication-status restriction alone (no language limit, or a justified one); the decision should say whether it covers these.

decisions.wording: Statement and magnitude corrected against the sources: the large within-arm effect sizes (d = 3.4 to 5.5) are the 2026 review's alone, the two largest computed with an end-point SD of zero (the 2019 review's per-trial SMDs run from −1 to 0.91 and do not say what they compare); the aripiprazole placebo trial's settled symptoms come from the network meta-analysis, which excluded it as recovered, and its p value is 0.032 in the 2026 review and p < 0.005 or < 0.05 in the 2019 review; the 2019 review adds only that one placebo-controlled trial; the registry excludes schizophrenia, not schizoaffective disorder; the usual-care trial's registry shortened every time frame from 36 to 24 months in the same update that replaced the primary outcome. Anchor 20's extracted text is extended with that time-frame change, which AI reader 21 confirmed at that place (its targeted-check note). Plain text unchanged (says no more than the statement).
decisions.status: mixed kept, with the reason replaced (METHODS §6.4: several studies with inconsistent findings and no adequate explanation), as AI reader 21 argues: the only pair tested twice (aripiprazole against risperidone) has one null trial and one significant trial read in opposite directions; paliperidone beat placebo after the acute phase but not usual care on global severity; global and symptom ratings disagree within the usual-care trial; comparator, population, outcome and duration could explain this, but none has been tested. Not single study (several independent trials); not replicated (no comparison tested twice with a consistent, checkable direction: the two aripiprazole trials against no aripiprazole use different comparators, one is known only through reviews that report it inconsistently, and the other switched its primary outcome after the trial ended). Reader 19's reason (differing populations, outcomes and risk of bias) describes indirectness and risk of bias, not inconsistency, and is dropped.
decisions.grade: Very low unchanged. Inconsistency 0 → −1, so that the domain matches the label (the downgrades now total five from high; the certainty is at its floor); the reasoning says the disagreements are counted under inconsistency and not again under indirectness. Risk of bias kept at −1: AI reader 21 finds −2 fair, and the reasoning already says the usual-care comparison alone would be −2; the certainty is very low either way. Indirectness −1 and imprecision −2 unchanged. Hall et al. (2026) is now cited as critically low.
decisions.verification: Unchanged, ai-anchored: not narrative-only (a network meta-analysis, two systematic reviews and a trial read in full); all seven references metadata-verified with a clear retraction check; all 21 anchors ai-checked.

questions.single study or mixed: Mixed, for inconsistent findings without a tested explanation (above).
questions.Chung 2026 description: Fair as worded: the registered primary outcome (relapse over 36 months) was unchanged from 2018 to version 13 (4 July 2025) and was replaced after primary completion (31 May 2024) and study completion (31 May 2025). Follow-up was not cut from 36 to 24 months first: the record history shows Outcome Measures changed only in versions 2, 14 and 15, and the comparison of versions 13 and 14 shows every 36-month time frame becoming 24 months in the same update that replaced relapse with the BPRS-24, so no 24-month design was registered before the outcome change. The claim now says so.

for_senior_author: Whether to rate risk of bias down two levels (AI reader 21; no effect on the certainty).
Optional: the article does not mention the registered outcome or its change (on the card, reporting issue 1); it is not in the claim because no anchor carries it.

Not added to the claim: the 2026 review gives a between-group p = 0.01 on the Simpson–Angus Scale for the aripiprazole–risperidone trial whose extrapyramidal ratings the 2019 review calls not different (now on the Hall card); the claim's side-effect sentence does not cite that measure.

decisions.wording: Statement: Murrie 2020's 22% is now an average over five estimates, with I² 96% and no prediction interval; the sentence that no study feature predicted transition is corrected (the review's P < .01 threshold covers its categorical subgroup analyses; older cohorts had somewhat lower rates in meta-regression, P = .03, possibly ecological), matching anchor 20 as corrected by AI reader 21. Magnitude likewise. Plain text rewritten as AI reader 21 proposes, leading with the spread (about 1 in 20 to about 2 in 5) and calling the 1 in 5 an average of five widely differing studies.
decisions.status: mixed kept: persistence 0% to 96% across studies and later schizophrenia diagnoses from about 5% to about 39%, with the only pooled amphetamine estimate at I² 96% and no moderator explaining it; the inconsistency is in size, not direction.
decisions.grade: Very low unchanged (start low; risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1); descriptive, never upgraded. The reasoning now cites Murrie 2020 as critically low (provisional) after adjudication of its card and says only the cohorts' average age was associated with transition.
decisions.verification: Unchanged, ai-anchored: a systematic review and a meta-analysis read in full; all references metadata-verified; all 22 anchors ai-checked.

questions.Murrie 2020's 22% leading: Fair in the statement, which gives I² 96%, the unnamed studies and the cocaine grouping in the same sentence; now also called an average without a prediction interval. In the plain text the spread now leads and the 1 in 5 is called an average, as AI reader 21 proposes.

for_senior_author: Not added: the meta-analysis's stated follow-up range (1 to 20 years) and the editors' calculation that its Thai figure is probably a share of those followed up; both are on the Murrie card, and either would need an anchor's extracted text extended before it goes into the claim.

decisions.wording: Statement: other drug and alcohol use, socio-economic position and family history were not adjusted for (other drug use is in the same database), not "not measured"; arrests reflect police contact and are not a validated measure of the amount used (the authors treat arrests as implying cumulative dose but could not assert dose dependence); the 10-year figures are Kaplan–Meier estimates. Magnitude likewise; plain text says an estimated 4 in 100. All three are AI reader 22's points, checked in the source.
decisions.status: replicated kept: the four adjusted studies of the 2019 meta-analysis, a New Zealand birth cohort and the Taiwan registry come from separate teams and data and agree in direction; the spread in size (1.33, 2.4, 5.28) follows comparator and adjustment, so it is not unexplained.
decisions.grade: Low unchanged (start low; no downgrades). No upgrade for large effect: Huang's HR stays large under its most adjusted model, but the remaining biases (no adjustment for other drugs, alcohol or socio-economic position against a group with no drug record; more contact with services after arrest) run away from the null. No upgrade for dose–response: arrests are counted over the whole follow-up and accumulate with time observed, and the printed trend p comes from five group rates.
decisions.verification: Unchanged, ai-anchored (not narrative-only; all 18 anchors ai-checked).

questions.\"not adjusted for\" rather than \"not m: Adopted (Huang 2022, Methods › Study population, 1st paragraph; Conclusions, 7th and 8th paragraphs).

decisions.wording: Statement: SUDORS counts methamphetamine as involved when the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death (main-text footnote §§); the report's largest increases with opioids are said of stimulant-involved deaths across racial and ethnic groups, not of T43.6 deaths alone; the cardiovascular contrast comes from the 46 states and DC with circumstance data, and both contrasts are crude. Plain text: medical examiners or coroners listed meth among the causes of about 31 in 100 overdose deaths, and this share cannot be compared directly with the 2019 one. Reasoning: Han et al. (2021) do give a 2019 opioid share, so the SUDORS share is the methamphetamine-specific share that the all-ages analysis (Zhu et al., 2025) lacked.
decisions.status: single study kept: the survey trend rests on one study, the death-record trend on three analyses of the same national death certificates (counted once, METHODS §6.3), and the SUDORS share on one pooled period of one system.
decisions.grade: Low unchanged (descriptive, starts low, never upgraded); coverage gaps and the expected undercount affect exact shares, not the order of magnitude or the direction of the rise.
decisions.verification: Unchanged, ai-anchored (primary data analyses; all 14 anchors ai-checked).

questions.\"found meth in\" → \"meth was one of th: Adopted in substance as "listed meth among the causes", which states what the record shows (the certifier's attribution, causing or contributing) without asserting cause for each death; the warning that the 2021–2024 share cannot be compared with the 2019 one is added to the plain text, as the statement already says.
questions.split the claim: Not recommended: each of the three parts rests on one body of data, so "single study" is exact for every part and the statement already says which system and period each figure comes from; a split is not clearly needed (compare senior decision 24).

decisions.wording: Statement and magnitude: the prediction model used adult smoking status (34 of 37 in the methamphetamine group smoked; a variable that can follow drug use), not just "smoking". Plain text adds that many in the methamphetamine group had also had alcohol or other drug problems, the study's most important omitted limit (AI reader 22's option; in the statement already). The authors' "difficult to disentangle" (not "cannot") is already in anchor 12 after the targeted check; the statement never said "cannot"; the study card is corrected.
decisions.status: replicated kept: the label rests on group means against norms (Simon 2010 and others); Dean 2018 reports no group mean against norms (scores standardized to its controls) and is from the same laboratory, with participants new for cognition.
decisions.grade: Very low unchanged (start low; risk of bias −1, imprecision −1); Dean 2018 changes no domain.
decisions.verification: Unchanged, ai-anchored (primary studies; all 13 anchors ai-checked).

questions.\"difficult to disentangle\": Already in anchor 12; the study card (key finding 13 and the polysubstance field) now says it too.
